1-D DP.probe: Your table uses O(n) space. Can you get the space down, and what property of your recurrence makes that possible?
1-D DP.listenFor: Notices the recurrence only looks back a constant number of states, so rolling variables suffice; states the new O(1) space and that time stays O(n).

1-D DP.probe: Now I don't just want the optimal value — I want the actual choices that produced it. What changes?
1-D DP.listenFor: Proposes either storing parent pointers per state or re-walking the table backward comparing dp values; notes reconstruction may force keeping the full O(n) table, trading back the space savings.

1-D DP.probe: Suppose the values arrive as a stream and you can't store the whole input. Can you still answer at each step?
1-D DP.listenFor: Recognizes that if the recurrence depends only on the last k states, streaming works with O(k) memory updated per element; identifies when full history would break this.

1-D DP.probe: Walk me through why memoization and bottom-up tabulation have the same time complexity here. When would you prefer one over the other?
1-D DP.listenFor: Explains both do O(1)-ish work per unique state so both are O(states x transition); prefers memoization when the state space is sparse or recursion is natural, tabulation to avoid stack depth and enable space optimization.

1-D DP.probe: What input would break your recursion depth if you'd written this top-down, and how do you defend against it?
1-D DP.listenFor: Quantifies that n around 10^5 blows typical stack limits; suggests converting to iterative bottom-up, raising the recursion limit cautiously, or an explicit stack, and mentions testing with worst-case depth.

1-D DP.probe: Turn this into a library function a teammate can call. What's the signature, and how do you handle empty input, negatives, or overflow?
1-D DP.listenFor: Defines a clear typed signature with documented behavior for empty and single-element inputs, states its complexity contract, validates arguments, and addresses overflow with wider types or modular arithmetic as appropriate.

BST Property.probe: Your solution assumes a valid BST. What happens if someone hands you a corrupted tree, and how would you detect that cheaply?
BST Property.listenFor: Notes the algorithm silently returns wrong answers on invalid trees; proposes an O(n) validation pass using min/max bounds or checking that inorder traversal is sorted before trusting BST-based pruning.

BST Property.probe: The tree is heavily skewed — essentially a linked list. What does that do to your complexity, and how do you fix it structurally?
BST Property.listenFor: States O(h) degrades from O(log n) to O(n) when skewed; names self-balancing structures (AVL, red-black) or rebuilding a balanced BST from sorted order as the fix.

BST Property.probe: Now the tree doesn't fit in memory — it lives on disk. How does your approach change?
BST Property.listenFor: Recognizes pointer-chasing per node is a disk seek; proposes B-tree style high-fanout nodes to cut height and I/O, and caching upper levels in memory.

BST Property.probe: How would you support repeated queries of this kind efficiently if the tree also receives inserts and deletes between queries?
BST Property.listenFor: Discusses augmenting nodes (subtree size, min/max) maintained during rotations, giving O(log n) per query and per update instead of recomputing, and the invariant-maintenance cost.

BST Property.probe: You used recursion. Convert the idea to an iterative version — what do you gain and what state do you have to carry?
BST Property.listenFor: Sketches iteration with an explicit stack or parent/successor threading, notes it avoids stack overflow on deep trees, and identifies exactly which bounds or predecessor state must be tracked manually.

BST Property.probe: Design this as a SortedMap API: what operations do you expose and what complexity do you promise for each?
BST Property.listenFor: Lists get, put, delete, floor, ceiling, rank, range queries; promises O(log n) contingent on balancing, and explains which BST augmentations each operation needs.

Backtracking.probe: What exactly is your branching factor and depth here, and what's the resulting worst-case time bound?
Backtracking.listenFor: Derives the bound as branching^depth or n! shaped, ties each factor to a concrete decision in the code, and distinguishes nodes explored from output size when solutions must be copied.

Backtracking.probe: The input can now contain duplicates. How do you avoid emitting duplicate solutions without a post-hoc set?
Backtracking.listenFor: Sorts the input and skips a candidate equal to its previous sibling at the same tree level, explaining why same-level skipping is correct while same-path reuse may still be allowed.

Backtracking.probe: This explores a huge tree. What pruning would you add, and how would you measure whether it actually helps?
Backtracking.listenFor: Proposes feasibility checks like remaining-sum bounds, constraint propagation, or ordering most-constrained-first; suggests counting recursive calls or timing on adversarial inputs to verify pruning pays off.

Backtracking.probe: Suppose I only need ONE valid solution, or just the COUNT of solutions, not all of them. Does your code change?
Backtracking.listenFor: For one solution, returns early by propagating a found flag; for counting, avoids materializing or copying paths; recognizes counting can sometimes switch to DP when subproblems overlap.

Backtracking.probe: Your recursion mutates a shared path list. What bug class does that invite, and how do you make the API safe for callers?
Backtracking.listenFor: Names aliasing: appending the live list yields results that later mutate; fixes by copying at leaf emission or using immutable path passing, and weighs the copy cost against safety.

Backtracking.probe: How would you parallelize this search across cores or machines?
Backtracking.listenFor: Splits the top-level branches into independent tasks, notes subtrees share no mutable state if the path is thread-local, and addresses work imbalance with work-stealing or dynamic task queues.

Binary Search.probe: Convince me your loop terminates and never misses the answer. What's your loop invariant?
Binary Search.listenFor: States the invariant precisely, e.g. answer always lies in [lo, hi], shows each iteration strictly shrinks the range, and explains how mid rounding plus the update rules avoid the infinite two-element loop.

Binary Search.probe: The array now contains duplicates and I want the FIRST occurrence. What changes in your code?
Binary Search.listenFor: Converts to a lower-bound search: on equality keep searching left by moving hi, never early-return on a match, and verify the final index after the loop.

Binary Search.probe: Classic question: what's wrong with mid = (lo + hi) / 2 in some languages, and what do you write instead?
Binary Search.listenFor: Identifies integer overflow when lo+hi exceeds the int max in fixed-width languages; writes lo + (hi - lo) / 2 and notes Python is immune but the habit still matters.

Binary Search.probe: The data no longer fits in RAM — it's a sorted file on disk or an API you can only probe by index. Does binary search survive?
Binary Search.listenFor: Yes: only O(log n) probes needed, each a seek or request; mentions latency dominates so log n round-trips matter, and considers interpolation search or caching if keys are uniformly distributed.

Binary Search.probe: Now the array is unbounded — you don't know n. How do you find the target?
Binary Search.listenFor: Doubles an upper bound with galloping/exponential search until the value is exceeded, then binary searches inside that window, keeping the total at O(log answer).

Binary Search.probe: Wrap this as a general search utility. What does the caller pass in, and how do you report a missing element?
Binary Search.listenFor: Accepts a comparator or key function and a bound flavor (first true / last false), returns an insertion point rather than a sentinel like -1, and documents the predicate-monotonicity precondition.

Binary Search on Answer.probe: How did you know binary search applies here at all? What property of the answer space are you relying on?
Binary Search on Answer.listenFor: Articulates monotonicity: the feasibility predicate is false then true (or vice versa) across the answer range, so the boundary is well-defined; explains why this specific check is monotone.

Binary Search on Answer.probe: What are your exact lower and upper bounds for the search, and what happens if you get them slightly wrong?
Binary Search on Answer.listenFor: Justifies bounds from the input (e.g. max element, sum of elements), notes a too-tight bound silently returns a wrong answer while a loose one only costs extra log-factor iterations, so err loose.

Binary Search on Answer.probe: Your feasibility check costs O(n). What's the total complexity, and can the check itself be made cheaper?
Binary Search on Answer.listenFor: States O(n log(range)) overall; explores incremental or precomputed structures like prefix sums to speed the check, and weighs whether the log factor of the range dominates.

Binary Search on Answer.probe: The answer is a real number now, not an integer. How do you decide when to stop?
Binary Search on Answer.listenFor: Iterates to a fixed epsilon or a fixed count of about 100 iterations; discusses precision pitfalls of comparing floats and why fixed iterations are more robust than epsilon on large ranges.

Binary Search on Answer.probe: Suppose the feasibility check is expensive and calls a remote service. How do you redesign to minimize checks?
Binary Search on Answer.listenFor: Notes log(range) calls is already near-optimal for a monotone predicate; adds caching of checked values, tightening bounds analytically first, and batching or parallel speculative probes if the service allows.

Binary Search on Answer.probe: Generalize this into a reusable 'search over answers' helper. What's the interface?
Binary Search on Answer.listenFor: Exposes lo, hi, and a predicate function, returns the boundary value, documents the monotonicity contract, and handles both integer and floating variants with a tolerance or iteration parameter.

Bit Manipulation.probe: Your trick relies on XOR properties. State them precisely and prove why your answer is correct.
Bit Manipulation.listenFor: States XOR is associative, commutative, x^x=0, x^0=x, and shows pairs cancel so only the odd-one-out survives; connects each property to a line of the solution.

Bit Manipulation.probe: What happens with negative numbers in your bitwise solution, especially in a language with arbitrary-precision integers like Python?
Bit Manipulation.listenFor: Explains two's complement assumptions break in Python since integers are unbounded; masks with 0xFFFFFFFF and converts back for sign, or notes languages where >> vs >>> matters.

Bit Manipulation.probe: Now the input is a stream of billions of numbers. Does your bit approach still work, and what's the memory footprint?
Bit Manipulation.listenFor: Notes XOR-style accumulators or per-bit counters need O(1) or O(32) state regardless of stream length, so it streams perfectly; contrasts with hash-set approaches that grow with distinct values.

Bit Manipulation.probe: How would you extend your approach if every element appears three times except one, instead of twice?
Bit Manipulation.listenFor: Moves from XOR to counting bits modulo 3 across 32 positions, or the two-variable ones/twos state machine, and explains why plain XOR no longer cancels triples.

Bit Manipulation.probe: Is your solution actually faster than the straightforward hash-map version? When would you choose each in production?
Bit Manipulation.listenFor: Same big-O time but O(1) space and better constants and cache behavior for bits; picks the readable hash version in application code and the bit version in hot paths or memory-constrained settings, with a comment either way.

Bit Manipulation.probe: Design a bitset/bitmask utility for a team. What operations do you expose and what edge cases do you document?
Bit Manipulation.listenFor: Offers set, clear, test, count, iterate-set-bits, and-or-xor; documents width and overflow behavior, out-of-range indices, and endianness or word-boundary handling in the backing array.

DP on Strings.probe: Your 2-D table is O(n*m) space. The strings are 50,000 characters each — now what?
DP on Strings.listenFor: Observes each row depends only on the previous row, so two rows give O(min(n,m)) space; flags that answer reconstruction then needs Hirschberg's divide-and-conquer or accepts value-only output.

DP on Strings.probe: I want the actual aligned subsequence or edit script, not just the length or count. How do you produce it?
DP on Strings.listenFor: Backtracks from dp[n][m] choosing which neighbor produced each value, emitting operations in reverse; notes this requires the full table or Hirschberg's technique under row-compression.

DP on Strings.probe: One string is tiny and one is huge — say 10 characters versus 10 million. Does that change your approach?
DP on Strings.listenFor: Puts the small string on the inner or column dimension for O(small) space, streams the huge string one character at a time, and notes total time O(n*m) is still fine because m is tiny.

DP on Strings.probe: The strings are Unicode with multi-byte characters and combining marks. What breaks?
DP on Strings.listenFor: Recognizes indexing by code unit versus code point versus grapheme cluster changes answers; proposes normalizing (NFC) and iterating grapheme clusters, and asks what equality should mean for the product.

DP on Strings.probe: Why is this problem not solvable greedily or with two pointers? Give me an input where the greedy fails.
DP on Strings.listenFor: Constructs a concrete counterexample where a locally best character match forfeits a longer global alignment, and ties it back to why overlapping subproblems demand DP.

DP on Strings.probe: Ship this as a text-diff utility. What API, what guarantees, and how do you test it?
DP on Strings.listenFor: Exposes diff(a, b) returning typed edit operations, documents O(n*m) cost and size limits, and tests with empty strings, identical strings, no-common-character pairs, and property-based round-trip application of the edit script.

DP on Subsequences.probe: How many states does your DP have, what does each state mean in plain English, and why is that set sufficient?
DP on Subsequences.listenFor: Defines the state as index plus remaining capacity or target, explains it captures everything the future needs (optimal substructure), and multiplies dimensions to justify the complexity.

DP on Subsequences.probe: The target sum is now 10^9. Your table doesn't fit. What are your options?
DP on Subsequences.listenFor: Recognizes pseudo-polynomial O(n*target) collapses; pivots to meet-in-the-middle for small n, value-based DP if values are small, or approximation, and can articulate why the problem is NP-hard in general.

DP on Subsequences.probe: Count the subsequences instead of deciding existence. What changes, and what new bug appears?
DP on Subsequences.listenFor: Switches boolean OR to additive counting; flags overflow needing modular arithmetic or big integers, and double-counting risks if identical elements or orderings aren't handled deliberately.

DP on Subsequences.probe: You iterate items outer, capacity inner. Why does the inner loop direction matter?
DP on Subsequences.listenFor: Explains descending capacity prevents reusing an item within the same iteration (0/1), while ascending allows unlimited reuse (complete knapsack); reversing it silently changes the problem being solved.

DP on Subsequences.probe: Elements can now be negative. Does your subset-sum DP survive?
DP on Subsequences.listenFor: Notes array-indexed-by-sum breaks with negatives; shifts by an offset over the full negative-to-positive range or moves to a dictionary-keyed DP, and rechecks the base case.

DP on Subsequences.probe: I need the actual chosen subset, and I need this callable repeatedly with different targets on the same array. Design that.
DP on Subsequences.listenFor: Precomputes the full reachability table once for O(1)-per-target queries up to max target, reconstructs by walking backward through decisions, and documents memory cost and rebuild triggers when the array changes.

Design.probe: Every operation you wrote is O(1) or O(log n) — prove it, including the ones that look O(1) but amortize.
Design.listenFor: Walks each public method, distinguishes worst-case from amortized (resizing, rehashing), and explains the amortization argument or how to de-amortize if the caller needs hard bounds.

Design.probe: Two threads now call your structure concurrently. What breaks first, and what's your locking strategy?
Design.listenFor: Identifies a specific race like a lost update between map and list mutation; discusses a coarse lock as the baseline, then finer strategies or lock-free options, and the invariants each protects.

Design.probe: Your structure now holds 100 million entries. What's the real memory footprint, and where does it go?
Design.listenFor: Accounts for per-entry overhead of nodes, pointers, and hash buckets rather than just payload bytes; proposes compaction like open addressing, primitive arrays, or sharding to disk with an eviction story.

Design.probe: What happens on bad input — get on a missing key, capacity zero, duplicate insert? Show me your contract.
Design.listenFor: Enumerates each edge with a deliberate documented behavior (sentinel, exception, or no-op), keeps invariants intact after failed operations, and mentions tests for each contract point.

Design.probe: How would you make this structure persist across restarts without killing your latency guarantees?
Design.listenFor: Separates the in-memory hot path from durability via write-ahead logging or periodic snapshots, discusses recovery-time replay, and what consistency is promised if a crash lands mid-operation.

Design.probe: A teammate wants to extend your design with one more operation — say, getRandom or a bulk delete. Which additions are cheap and which force a redesign?
Design.listenFor: Reasons from the chosen representation: which invariants the new op can piggyback on versus which auxiliary index it would need; shows the classic array-plus-map trick for getRandom or explains the cost honestly.

Divide & Conquer.probe: Write the recurrence for your algorithm and solve it. Which case of the Master Theorem is this?
Divide & Conquer.listenFor: States T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) with correct a, b, f from the code, identifies the Master Theorem case, and derives the final bound rather than reciting it.

Divide & Conquer.probe: What is your recursion depth in the worst case, and could it blow the stack? How do you harden that?
Divide & Conquer.listenFor: Distinguishes balanced O(log n) depth from adversarial O(n) (e.g. bad pivots), proposes randomization or median-of-medians, tail-recursing into the larger half only, or an explicit stack.

Divide & Conquer.probe: The combine step is where your cost lives. Can you cheapen it, or trade combine work for divide work?
Divide & Conquer.listenFor: Analyzes the merge cost concretely, considers pre-sorting once, in-place merging trade-offs, or restructuring so subresults carry extra info that makes combining O(1) or O(log n).

Divide & Conquer.probe: Parallelize this across 8 cores. What speedup do you actually expect and why not 8x?
Divide & Conquer.listenFor: Notes subproblems are independent so fork-join fits naturally, but the combine step and small-subproblem overhead serialize; invokes Amdahl's law and a cutoff to sequential below a threshold size.

Divide & Conquer.probe: The data is on disk in chunks that don't fit in memory together. Adapt your algorithm.
Divide & Conquer.listenFor: Maps the approach to external processing: solve chunks that fit in RAM, then k-way merge or combine with a heap; counts I/O passes rather than comparisons as the real cost.

Divide & Conquer.probe: For small subproblems, is recursing actually the right call? What would you do in production code?
Divide & Conquer.listenFor: Switches to a simple O(n^2)-style base case below a tuned threshold because constants and call overhead dominate; mentions benchmarking to pick the cutoff, as real sort libraries do.

Fast & Slow Pointers.probe: Prove to me the two pointers must meet if there's a cycle — why can't the fast one jump over the slow one?
Fast & Slow Pointers.listenFor: Argues the gap shrinks by exactly one each step once both are in the cycle, so a meeting is forced within one cycle length; the relative speed of 1 makes jumping over impossible.

Fast & Slow Pointers.probe: After they meet, you reset one pointer to the head. Why does that find the cycle start? Show the math.
Fast & Slow Pointers.listenFor: Derives the distance relation: head-to-entry distance equals meeting-point-to-entry distance modulo cycle length, from 2(a+b) = a+b+kc, so equal-speed walking meets at the entry.

Fast & Slow Pointers.probe: Could you have solved this with a hash set of visited nodes instead? Compare the two honestly.
Fast & Slow Pointers.listenFor: Notes the hash set is simpler and finds the start directly but costs O(n) memory; Floyd is O(1) space with the same O(n) time; picks based on constraints and code clarity.

Fast & Slow Pointers.probe: The linked list is now an array where a[i] tells you the next index, values 1..n. Where does the cycle come from and what does finding it give you?
Fast & Slow Pointers.listenFor: Maps the duplicate-number problem onto cycle detection: pigeonhole forces a cycle, the cycle entry is the duplicate, and the array is never modified, satisfying read-only O(1)-space constraints.

Fast & Slow Pointers.probe: What does your code do on an empty list, a single node, or a list with no cycle? Walk each path.
Fast & Slow Pointers.listenFor: Traces the guard conditions: fast or fast.next hitting null exits cleanly with a no-cycle answer, single node with self-loop still detected; shows no null dereference on any path.

Fast & Slow Pointers.probe: Generalize: what other problems does the fast/slow technique solve, and what's the common thread?
Fast & Slow Pointers.listenFor: Names middle-of-list, palindrome check, happy number, cycle in function iteration; the thread is detecting periodicity or fractional positions in a sequence you can only walk forward with O(1) memory.

Graph Traversal.probe: Your complexity claim is O(V+E). Point to the exact lines that guarantee no vertex or edge is processed twice.
Graph Traversal.listenFor: Points to the visited set checked before enqueue/recurse (not after dequeue only), explains marking on discovery versus on processing, and how adjacency iteration touches each edge a constant number of times.

Graph Traversal.probe: The graph doesn't fit in memory — neighbors come from an API call. How does your traversal change?
Graph Traversal.listenFor: Keeps frontier plus visited in memory and fetches neighbors lazily; discusses batching or caching requests, and if visited itself is too big, sharded sets, Bloom filters with false-positive caveats, or disk-backed frontiers.

Graph Traversal.probe: You used recursion for DFS. What input kills it, and what does the iterative rewrite look like?
Graph Traversal.listenFor: A path-shaped graph of 10^5+ nodes overflows the stack; rewrites with an explicit stack and explains the subtlety of when to mark visited and how to simulate post-order if needed.

Graph Traversal.probe: The graph is now directed, or now has disconnected components. Which of your assumptions break?
Graph Traversal.listenFor: Audits assumptions: needs an outer loop over all vertices for components, direction changes reachability so undirected symmetry tricks fail, and parent-skipping cycle checks stop working on directed graphs.

Graph Traversal.probe: How would you find connected components repeatedly as edges keep getting added? Is re-traversal the best tool?
Graph Traversal.listenFor: Recognizes incremental connectivity is Union-Find territory with near-O(1) amortized updates versus O(V+E) per re-traversal; notes edge deletions make it much harder and names offline or link-cut approaches exist.

Graph Traversal.probe: Package your traversal as a reusable graph library function. What does the caller provide and what do you return?
Graph Traversal.listenFor: Takes a neighbor function or adjacency structure plus start nodes and visitor callbacks, documents visitation order guarantees and cycle safety, and returns discovery data like parents and distances rather than printing.

Greedy.probe: Greedy algorithms are usually wrong. Why is yours right? Sketch the exchange argument.
Greedy.listenFor: Gives an exchange or staying-ahead argument: any optimal solution can be transformed to include the greedy choice without loss, or cites a matroid structure; a bare 'it seems locally best' is not accepted.

Greedy.probe: Give me a variant of this problem where your greedy strategy breaks, and the input that proves it.
Greedy.listenFor: Constructs a concrete counterexample, e.g. coin change with denominations 1,3,4 and target 6, and identifies which structural property the variant lost that the proof needed.

Greedy.probe: Your sort dominates the runtime. Can you avoid the full sort?
Greedy.listenFor: Considers whether only the top-k matter (heap for O(n log k)), bucket or counting sort when the key range is small, or whether the greedy truly needs total order versus a partial one.

Greedy.probe: The items now arrive online — you must decide on each irrevocably before seeing the rest. Does greedy survive?
Greedy.listenFor: Distinguishes offline from online: names competitive-ratio thinking, whether any algorithm can be optimal online, and what regret or approximation the natural online greedy achieves.

Greedy.probe: Two items tie on your sort key. Can tie-breaking order change the answer, and how do you make the output deterministic?
Greedy.listenFor: Analyzes whether ties affect optimality or only which optimal solution is produced; adds a documented secondary key for deterministic, testable output and mentions stable sort behavior.

Greedy.probe: If I perturb one input value slightly, your greedy answer can change completely. Is that a problem, and how would you flag low-confidence answers in a product?
Greedy.listenFor: Acknowledges greedy decisions can be brittle near ties, suggests reporting margins or sensitivity (how close the decision boundary was), and validating with a DP or brute-force oracle on small inputs in tests.

Hashing.probe: You keep saying O(1) lookup. When is that a lie, and what's the true worst case?
Hashing.listenFor: Explains expected O(1) rests on good hash distribution; adversarial or colliding keys degrade to O(n) per op (or O(log n) with tree buckets), and mentions load factor and rehashing amortization.

Hashing.probe: The input is now 100x bigger than RAM. Your hash map doesn't fit. Redesign.
Hashing.listenFor: Partitions by hash into disk-resident shards processed one at a time, or streams with approximate structures like Count-Min or Bloom filters when exactness is negotiable, stating error bounds.

Hashing.probe: What are you actually using as the key here — and what goes wrong with floating-point keys or mutable objects?
Hashing.listenFor: Flags float equality and NaN pitfalls, proposes canonicalizing (rounding, ratios in lowest terms with sign convention); notes mutable keys break bucket location invariants after mutation.

Hashing.probe: Someone feeds your service adversarial keys engineered to collide. What happens and how do you defend?
Hashing.listenFor: Describes hash-flooding DoS turning ops O(n); defends with randomized/seeded or SipHash-style hashing, per-request limits, or tree-based fallback buckets like Java 8's HashMap.

Hashing.probe: Could sorting have solved this instead of hashing? Compare the two solutions end to end.
Hashing.listenFor: Compares O(n) average with O(n) space against O(n log n) with O(1) extra space and better cache behavior and determinism; picks based on memory limits, adversarial inputs, and whether output order matters.

Hashing.probe: Your prefix-count trick with the hash map — explain why you insert the prefix BEFORE or AFTER the lookup, and what bug the wrong order causes.
Hashing.listenFor: Explains lookup-then-insert prevents counting a zero-length or self-matching subarray incorrectly, walks the empty-prefix initialization (map[0]=1) and shows the off-by-one a wrong order produces.

Heap / Top-K.probe: Why a heap of size k rather than sorting everything? And why a MIN-heap for top-k largest?
Heap / Top-K.listenFor: Contrasts O(n log k) and O(k) space with O(n log n) sort; explains the min-heap's root is the weakest current member, so eviction is O(log k) when a better candidate arrives.

Heap / Top-K.probe: The elements now arrive as an endless stream and k is fixed. What does your memory profile look like over time?
Heap / Top-K.listenFor: Notes the size-k heap is exactly the streaming answer: O(k) memory forever, O(log k) per element, and the current top-k is queryable at any moment.

Heap / Top-K.probe: Could quickselect beat your heap here? When would you pick each?
Heap / Top-K.listenFor: Quickselect is O(n) average, in-place, but offline-only, order-destroying, and O(n^2) worst case without median-of-medians; heap wins for streaming, stability of guarantees, or when k is small.

Heap / Top-K.probe: Now I need to DELETE arbitrary elements from the heap, not just the root. What breaks?
Heap / Top-K.listenFor: Standard binary heaps lack O(log n) arbitrary delete without a position index; proposes an index map maintained through swaps, or lazy deletion with a tombstone set checked at pop time.

Heap / Top-K.probe: k is close to n — say k = n-5. Is your approach still the right one?
Heap / Top-K.listenFor: Flips the problem: find the (n-k) smallest with a tiny heap instead, or just sort; shows awareness that O(n log k) approaches O(n log n) and constants decide.

Heap / Top-K.probe: Design a reusable TopK tracker class for a metrics service. What's the API and what are the concurrency concerns?
Heap / Top-K.listenFor: Offers add(item, score), topK() snapshot, maybe decay or windowing; discusses snapshot consistency under concurrent adds, locking or sharding per key, and memory bounds documentation.

Interval / Partition DP.probe: Your DP is O(n^3). Walk me through where each factor of n comes from, and whether any can be shaved.
Interval / Partition DP.listenFor: Attributes n^2 to interval endpoints and n to the split point; mentions Knuth's optimization or monotonicity of optimal split points can drop it to O(n^2) when the quadrangle inequality holds.

Interval / Partition DP.probe: Why must you iterate intervals by increasing LENGTH? What goes wrong with a naive left-to-right sweep?
Interval / Partition DP.listenFor: Explains dp[i][j] depends on strictly shorter intervals inside it, so length-order guarantees dependencies are ready; a plain row sweep reads uninitialized or stale states.

Interval / Partition DP.probe: What is your base case, and what does dp[i][i] (or an empty interval) mean physically in this problem?
Interval / Partition DP.listenFor: Grounds the base case in the problem story — a single element or empty range costs zero or its own value — and shows the recurrence degenerates correctly at length 1 and 2.

Interval / Partition DP.probe: n is now 5,000. Your O(n^3) is 125 billion operations. What are your options?
Interval / Partition DP.listenFor: Quantifies infeasibility honestly; offers Knuth/divide-and-conquer optimization if the cost function qualifies, problem-specific greedy or approximation, or challenges whether the full generality is needed.

Interval / Partition DP.probe: I want the actual optimal partition or merge order, not just its cost. How do you recover it?
Interval / Partition DP.listenFor: Stores the argmin split point per interval in a companion table and reconstructs recursively top-down, or re-derives splits by testing which k achieves dp[i][j]; notes the memory already exists.

Interval / Partition DP.probe: The 'burst balloons' style trick — thinking about the LAST element removed instead of the first. Why does that direction make the subproblems independent?
Interval / Partition DP.listenFor: Explains that fixing the last action makes both sides' boundaries known constants, so left and right intervals no longer interact; choosing the first action leaves future dependencies that entangle subproblems.

Intervals.probe: Everything hinged on sorting. Sorted by start or by end — and would the other choice still be correct here?
Intervals.listenFor: States which key the algorithm needs and why: end-time sorting powers greedy selection proofs, start-time powers merging sweeps; gives a counterexample where the wrong key fails.

Intervals.probe: Do your comparisons treat [1,3] and [3,5] as overlapping? Which did the problem want, and where in the code is that decision?
Intervals.listenFor: Pinpoints the boundary comparison operator, articulates closed versus half-open interval semantics, and shows the single character that flips touching-counts-as-overlap behavior.

Intervals.probe: Intervals now arrive one at a time and I need the merged set maintained continuously. What structure do you reach for?
Intervals.listenFor: Proposes an ordered map or balanced tree keyed by start, finding neighbors with floor/ceiling to merge in O(log n) per insert, and mentions the interval-tree alternative for stabbing queries.

Intervals.probe: There are a million intervals but I only ever query 'how many cover point x'. Change your approach.
Intervals.listenFor: Switches to a difference array or sorted event list of +1/-1 boundaries with prefix sums, answering point queries by binary search in O(log n) after O(n log n) preprocessing.

Intervals.probe: What edge cases would you test before shipping this — give me five concrete inputs.
Intervals.listenFor: Lists empty input, a single interval, fully nested intervals, exact-touching boundaries, duplicates, and reversed or zero-length intervals; explains what each one is designed to catch.

Intervals.probe: Timestamps are now floating-point or timezone-bearing datetimes. What new bugs appear?
Intervals.listenFor: Flags float equality on boundaries, DST making wall-clock intervals non-monotonic; recommends epoch integers or UTC normalization at the boundary of the system and documents the convention.

Knapsack DP.probe: Your runtime is O(n*W). Is that polynomial? Careful — this is a trick question.
Knapsack DP.listenFor: Identifies pseudo-polynomial time: W's magnitude is exponential in its bit length, so knapsack stays NP-hard; explains why this matters when capacities get astronomically large.

Knapsack DP.probe: Capacity W is now 10^12. The table is impossible. What do you do?
Knapsack DP.listenFor: Offers value-based DP O(n * total value) if values are small, meet-in-the-middle for n up to about 40, FPTAS approximation with bounded error, or branch-and-bound; matches technique to the regime.

Knapsack DP.probe: You compressed to a 1-D array. Explain the loop direction, and what different problem the reversed loop solves.
Knapsack DP.listenFor: Backward capacity iteration ensures each item used at most once; forward iteration reuses items unbounded, silently turning 0/1 knapsack into complete knapsack — states this as the classic trap.

Knapsack DP.probe: I need the chosen item set, not just the best value — but you compressed the table. Reconcile that.
Knapsack DP.listenFor: Either retains the full 2-D table for backtracking, keeps per-cell choice bitsets or parent info, or re-solves subproblems recursively; acknowledges the space-versus-reconstruction trade honestly.

Knapsack DP.probe: Items arrive online and you must accept or reject each immediately. What can you still guarantee?
Knapsack DP.listenFor: Recognizes online knapsack has no constant competitive ratio in general; discusses threshold-based policies under random order or known value-density ranges, and clearly separates guarantees from heuristics.

Knapsack DP.probe: Add a second constraint — say weight AND volume. How does your DP scale, and when does this stop being practical?
Knapsack DP.listenFor: Extends state to dp[w][v] making it O(n*W*V), notes the curse of dimensionality, and suggests Lagrangian relaxation, scalarization, or pruning dominated states when dimensions multiply out of reach.

Linked List Manipulation.probe: Rewrite this using a dummy/sentinel head. What entire class of bugs does that eliminate?
Linked List Manipulation.listenFor: Shows the sentinel unifies the head-modification case with the middle case, removing special-cased null checks for deleting or inserting at the head, and returns dummy.next at the end.

Linked List Manipulation.probe: Walk me through your pointer updates on a two-node list, drawing the state after every assignment. Any order that breaks it?
Linked List Manipulation.listenFor: Traces each assignment showing no node is orphaned; identifies the exact reordering that loses the rest of the list and why saving next before rewiring is load-bearing.

Linked List Manipulation.probe: Your reversal is iterative. Do it recursively — and then tell me why production code might still prefer your first version.
Linked List Manipulation.listenFor: Writes the recursive version correctly, then notes O(n) stack depth risks overflow on long lists and the iterative O(1)-space version is strictly safer for unbounded input.

Linked List Manipulation.probe: The list may contain a cycle due to upstream corruption. Your traversal now hangs. How do you harden it?
Linked List Manipulation.listenFor: Adds cycle detection (Floyd or a step-count bound against a known max length) before or during traversal, and discusses failing loudly versus best-effort processing when corruption is found.

Linked List Manipulation.probe: Why does this problem use a linked list at all? When would an array-based solution dominate?
Linked List Manipulation.listenFor: Articulates the real trade: O(1) splice given a node reference versus terrible cache locality and O(n) indexing; notes arrays win in most modern-hardware scenarios unless splicing mid-structure is the hot operation.

Linked List Manipulation.probe: Design this as a safe public API: what happens on an empty list, k larger than the length, or a null input?
Linked List Manipulation.listenFor: Documents each contract explicitly — no-op, clamp, or raised error — validates before mutating so failures leave the list intact, and adds length-check or modulo normalization for oversized k.

Math & Number Theory.probe: Your answer can exceed 64-bit range. Where exactly can overflow happen, and how do you handle it in a fixed-width language?
Math & Number Theory.listenFor: Locates the specific multiplication or accumulation at risk, applies modular reduction at every step rather than at the end, or uses 128-bit/big-integer types, and explains why intermediate values matter.

Math & Number Theory.probe: You're taking results mod p. Now the problem needs division. What do you do?
Math & Number Theory.listenFor: Explains division becomes multiplication by the modular inverse, computed via Fermat's little theorem when p is prime or extended Euclid otherwise, and notes the inverse fails when gcd isn't 1.

Math & Number Theory.probe: Prove your loop bound — why is checking up to sqrt(n) sufficient, or why does your exponentiation take O(log n) steps?
Math & Number Theory.listenFor: Gives the pairing argument that any factor above sqrt(n) has a partner below it, or shows fast exponentiation halves the exponent each step, tying the math to the loop structure.

Math & Number Theory.probe: Now I need this computed for a million different queries, not one. What do you precompute?
Math & Number Theory.listenFor: Amortizes with sieves for primes/smallest-factor, factorial and inverse-factorial tables for combinatorics, answering each query in O(1) or O(log n); states the precomputation cost and memory.

Math & Number Theory.probe: Floating point crept into your solution (sqrt, pow, log). Where does it betray you, and what's the integer-safe version?
Math & Number Theory.listenFor: Names precision failures near perfect squares or large magnitudes, replaces with integer binary search or exact integer arithmetic, and verifies candidate answers with integer multiplication.

Math & Number Theory.probe: n can be negative or zero now. Audit your solution — which identities silently assumed positivity?
Math & Number Theory.listenFor: Rechecks modulo sign behavior across languages (negative % in C++ vs Python), gcd and division conventions for negatives, and zero-input degeneracies, patching each with explicit normalization.

Matrix Traversal.probe: You modified the input matrix in place to mark visits. When is that unacceptable, and what's the fix costing you?
Matrix Traversal.listenFor: Notes callers may need the input intact and concurrent readers break; alternatives are a separate visited grid at O(m*n) space or restoring cells afterward, and states the trade explicitly.

Matrix Traversal.probe: The matrix is a million by a million but only a few thousand cells are interesting. Does your approach survive?
Matrix Traversal.listenFor: Switches to a sparse representation — a dict or set of occupied coordinates — traversing neighbors of known cells only, making cost proportional to interesting cells not the full grid.

Matrix Traversal.probe: Your directions array covers 4 neighbors. The problem shifts to 8-directional or to a hex grid. How brittle is your code?
Matrix Traversal.listenFor: Shows the direction vectors are a single data-driven list so the change is one line; flags any logic that hard-coded four-ness, like corner or parity assumptions, that must be re-audited.

Matrix Traversal.probe: Rows arrive one at a time from a stream — you never hold the full grid. Which of these problems can you still solve?
Matrix Traversal.listenFor: Identifies DP-style problems needing only the previous row as streamable with O(width) memory; recognizes flood-fill or global-connectivity problems fundamentally need more, or Union-Find on two rows at a time.

Matrix Traversal.probe: Where can your row/column indices go wrong — walk me through your bounds checks on a 1x1 and a 1xN matrix.
Matrix Traversal.listenFor: Traces boundary guards on degenerate shapes, checks row length taken from the right dimension (ragged or transposed confusion), and confirms no index arithmetic mixes rows with columns.

Matrix Traversal.probe: Recursion for flood fill on a 1000x1000 grid of one region — what happens and what's your production version?
Matrix Traversal.listenFor: Predicts stack overflow at up to a million deep recursion; converts to an explicit stack or BFS queue, and mentions scanline fill as the cache-friendlier optimization real image editors use.

Monotonic Stack.probe: Your loop has a nested while — convince me the total time is still O(n).
Monotonic Stack.listenFor: Gives the amortized argument: each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so total pop work across the whole run is O(n); charges the inner loop to elements, not iterations.

Monotonic Stack.probe: Decreasing or increasing stack — which did you use, and how do you decide when facing a new problem of this family?
Monotonic Stack.listenFor: Maps the question type to the invariant: next-greater needs a decreasing stack, next-smaller increasing; explains you keep exactly the elements whose answer is still unknown.

Monotonic Stack.probe: Duplicated values: does your comparison use strict or non-strict inequality, and what double-counting bug does the wrong choice cause?
Monotonic Stack.listenFor: Shows the strictness choice determines which side owns equal elements in span or subarray-counting problems; demonstrates the double-count or miss on an input with repeated values.

Monotonic Stack.probe: You store indices on the stack, not values. Why is that the stronger choice?
Monotonic Stack.listenFor: Indices recover both value and position for distances, widths, and areas; values alone lose position information, and the index version subsumes the value version at no cost.

Monotonic Stack.probe: The array becomes a stream and I need next-greater answers as elements arrive. Which direction of the problem is answerable online?
Monotonic Stack.listenFor: Notes an arriving element resolves answers for earlier pending elements — so next-greater is answered with a delay, emitted at pop time; asking about future elements immediately is impossible by definition.

Monotonic Stack.probe: What happens if I ask for previous-greater AND next-greater for every element — do you need two passes?
Monotonic Stack.listenFor: Either runs two symmetric passes, or shows the single-pass insight: at pop time the popped element learns its next-greater (current) and its previous-greater (new stack top) simultaneously.

Queue & BFS.probe: Why does BFS guarantee shortest path here — and what single change to the problem would break that guarantee?
Queue & BFS.listenFor: Ties correctness to uniform edge weights and level-order expansion; recognizes weighted edges break it, requiring Dijkstra, or 0/1 weights allowing deque-based 0-1 BFS.

Queue & BFS.probe: Where exactly do you mark a node visited — at enqueue or at dequeue — and why does the difference matter?
Queue & BFS.listenFor: Marks at enqueue to prevent the same node entering the queue multiple times; explains the dequeue-marking version still terminates but can balloon the queue exponentially in dense graphs.

Queue & BFS.probe: How are you tracking BFS levels/distance? Show me two ways and their trade-offs.
Queue & BFS.listenFor: Describes level-size batching (process len(queue) nodes per round) versus storing distance with each node; notes batching keeps nodes lean while pairing is simpler for early exit on target.

Queue & BFS.probe: The state space is enormous — say, word ladders or puzzle states. What optimization halves the effective depth?
Queue & BFS.listenFor: Proposes bidirectional BFS expanding the smaller frontier, cutting b^d to roughly 2*b^(d/2); discusses frontier-meeting detection and why always expanding the smaller side matters.

Queue & BFS.probe: Multiple starting sources, like rotten oranges. How does your BFS change and why is it still one traversal?
Queue & BFS.listenFor: Seeds all sources into the queue at distance zero before starting; explains this computes distance-to-nearest-source for every node in a single O(V+E) pass, no per-source repetition.

Queue & BFS.probe: The frontier itself no longer fits in memory. What are your options?
Queue & BFS.listenFor: Mentions iterative deepening DFS trading time for O(d) memory, bidirectional search shrinking frontiers, disk-backed frontier queues with delayed duplicate detection, or compressing visited with Bloom filters plus caveats.

Shortest Path.probe: Why Dijkstra here and not plain BFS — and what property of the input would let you fall back to BFS?
Shortest Path.listenFor: Weights make level-order invalid; uniform weights reduce to BFS, 0/1 weights to deque BFS; articulates Dijkstra's greedy settlement invariant that finalized distances never improve.

Shortest Path.probe: One edge weight is negative. What breaks in your algorithm, and what do you switch to at what cost?
Shortest Path.listenFor: Explains Dijkstra's settled-node assumption fails with negative edges; switches to Bellman-Ford O(VE) with negative-cycle detection, or SPFA caveats, and notes negative cycles make 'shortest' undefined.

Shortest Path.probe: Your priority queue holds stale entries after relaxations. How does your implementation handle them, and what's the alternative?
Shortest Path.listenFor: Describes lazy deletion — skip popped entries worse than the recorded distance — versus decrease-key with an indexed heap; states the O((V+E) log V) bound survives lazy deletion.

Shortest Path.probe: I need shortest paths between ALL pairs now, on a graph with 400 nodes. And what if it's 100,000 nodes?
Shortest Path.listenFor: Picks Floyd-Warshall O(V^3) for small dense graphs, repeated Dijkstra O(V E log V) for sparse; for huge graphs discusses whether all-pairs is even storable and pivots to on-demand or landmark/CH techniques.

Shortest Path.probe: The graph is a road network and users query routes interactively. Cold Dijkstra per query is too slow. What do real systems do?
Shortest Path.listenFor: Mentions bidirectional Dijkstra, A* with admissible heuristics like landmarks or great-circle distance, and preprocessing families like contraction hierarchies trading offline work for millisecond queries.

Shortest Path.probe: State as a node: the problem adds a constraint like 'at most k stops' or 'carrying a key'. How do you model it?
Shortest Path.listenFor: Expands the graph to (node, constraint-state) product space, runs the same algorithm over it, and analyzes the multiplied size; recognizes this as the standard layered-graph technique.

Sliding Window.probe: Prove your window never misses the optimal answer — why is it safe to move the left pointer and never look back?
Sliding Window.listenFor: Articulates the monotonicity invariant: once the window is invalid, no extension of that left endpoint can become valid or better, so discarding it is safe; connects this to why the technique applies at all.

Sliding Window.probe: Each element enters and leaves the window once — so O(n). Show me a problem variant where the sliding window silently becomes O(n^2) or just wrong.
Sliding Window.listenFor: Recognizes windows fail when validity isn't monotone — e.g. sums with negative numbers — because shrinking doesn't monotonically fix violations; names prefix-sum-plus-hash as the correct fallback.

Sliding Window.probe: The stream is infinite and the window is time-based — 'last 5 minutes' — not count-based. Redesign your bookkeeping.
Sliding Window.listenFor: Uses a deque or ring of timestamped entries evicted by age on each query or arrival, discusses memory proportional to window contents, and approximate summaries when even that is too large.

Sliding Window.probe: Your window tracks a max or min as it slides. Doing that naively is O(n) per step — fix it.
Sliding Window.listenFor: Introduces the monotonic deque: amortized O(1) per slide, front holds the extremum, elements dominated by newer arrivals are evicted from the back; explains why each element enters and leaves once.

Sliding Window.probe: 'At most k distinct' worked with your window. Now I ask for EXACTLY k distinct. Why doesn't the window apply directly, and what's the trick?
Sliding Window.listenFor: Explains exactly-k lacks monotonicity but decomposes: exactly(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k-1), reusing the working window function twice; can articulate why the subtraction is correct.

Sliding Window.probe: Package your window logic as a reusable stream-metrics class. What's the API and what invariants must every method preserve?
Sliding Window.listenFor: Exposes add(item) and query() with documented complexity, keeps eviction and aggregate maintenance internal and consistent after every call, and tests boundary conditions like empty windows and single elements.

Sorting & Prefix.probe: You sorted the input, which cost O(n log n). Is the sort actually necessary, or is there a linear-time structure hiding here?
Sorting & Prefix.listenFor: Interrogates whether full order was needed: counting or bucket sort for small ranges, a single min/max pass, or a hash-based approach; justifies the sort if comparisons are truly required.

Sorting & Prefix.probe: Your prefix-sum array answers range queries in O(1). Now the underlying array gets point UPDATES too. What structure do you migrate to?
Sorting & Prefix.listenFor: Names Fenwick/BIT or segment tree giving O(log n) for both update and range query; contrasts with O(n) rebuild per update, and picks based on operation mix and implementation budget.

Sorting & Prefix.probe: The values are floats and your prefix sums accumulate over a billion elements. What's quietly going wrong?
Sorting & Prefix.listenFor: Identifies floating-point error accumulation and catastrophic cancellation in prefix differences; suggests Kahan summation, pairwise summation, or integer fixed-point representation of the domain.

Sorting & Prefix.probe: Sort stability — did your solution depend on it? Construct a case where an unstable sort changes your answer.
Sorting & Prefix.listenFor: Understands stability preserves original order among equal keys; builds a concrete case with tied keys where output order or index-based answers differ, and names which library sorts guarantee stability.

Sorting & Prefix.probe: The data is 10x RAM and must be sorted. Walk me through how you'd actually do it.
Sorting & Prefix.listenFor: Describes external merge sort: sort RAM-sized runs, spill to disk, k-way merge with a heap; counts I/O passes, mentions replacement selection or larger fan-in to reduce passes.

Sorting & Prefix.probe: You built a 1-D prefix sum. Extend it to 2-D for submatrix-sum queries — write the inclusion-exclusion carefully.
Sorting & Prefix.listenFor: Constructs P[i][j] with the add-two-subtract-one-overlap recurrence and queries with four-term inclusion-exclusion; handles the zero-row/column padding that kills off-by-one errors.

Stack.probe: Why is a stack the right structure here — what LIFO property of the problem is it mirroring?
Stack.listenFor: Connects the structure to the problem's nesting or most-recent-first nature — innermost brackets close first, latest operation undone first — rather than describing the stack mechanically.

Stack.probe: What does your code do on adversarial input — unbalanced closers, an empty string, input that's all openers?
Stack.listenFor: Walks the pop-on-empty guard, the end-of-input nonempty-stack check, and confirms both failure directions (extra closers, unclosed openers) are caught; lists the tests proving it.

Stack.probe: Your stack can grow to O(n). Is there a variant of this problem solvable in O(1) space, and what capability do you lose?
Stack.listenFor: Notes single-bracket-type matching reduces to a counter; explains multiple types or content reconstruction genuinely need the stack, distinguishing recognition from parsing power.

Stack.probe: Extend your bracket matcher into a real expression parser with operators and precedence. What's the architecture?
Stack.listenFor: Describes two-stack shunting-yard or recursive descent with a precedence table, handling parentheses, unary minus, and associativity; identifies error reporting with positions as part of the design.

Stack.probe: The input arrives in chunks over a network and you must report 'broken' as early as possible. Adapt your solution.
Stack.listenFor: Keeps the stack alive across chunks as streaming state, fails fast the moment a mismatch appears rather than at end, and defines what to emit if the stream ends mid-nesting.

Stack.probe: Implement your stack solution without recursion where you'd used it, or vice versa — and explain what the call stack was doing for you.
Stack.listenFor: Demonstrates the equivalence: recursion's call stack held the same pending state; converts between the two and notes explicit stacks give control over depth limits and iteration order.

String Matching.probe: Your matcher runs in O(n*m) worst case. Construct the adversarial input that hits it, then name what fixes it.
String Matching.listenFor: Builds a degenerate case like aaaa...b patterns forcing repeated re-scanning; names KMP, Z-algorithm, or rolling-hash approaches achieving O(n+m) and sketches why they avoid re-examination.

String Matching.probe: Explain the failure function / rolling hash you used — what is it actually storing, and why does that avoid re-comparing characters?
String Matching.listenFor: For KMP: the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix lets the pattern shift without losing a possible match; for hashing: O(1) window re-hash with collision probability analysis and verification strategy.

String Matching.probe: Now there are 10,000 patterns to find in one text. Running your matcher 10,000 times is out. What's the right tool?
String Matching.listenFor: Names Aho-Corasick building a trie with failure links for all patterns, matching in O(text + total pattern length + matches); or suffix automata/arrays when the text is fixed and patterns vary.

String Matching.probe: The text is streaming — you see each character once and can't store the text. Which of your algorithms survive?
String Matching.listenFor: Recognizes KMP and Aho-Corasick are naturally streaming with O(pattern) state; rolling hash also works; anything requiring backward scanning or the full text dies, and says so explicitly.

String Matching.probe: Your rolling-hash solution — what's the collision story, and would you ship it without verification?
String Matching.listenFor: Quantifies collision probability with modulus size, mentions birthday effects and adversarial anti-hash inputs, and either verifies candidate matches character-by-character or uses double hashing with justified confidence.

String Matching.probe: Case-insensitivity, Unicode normalization, and 'whole word only' are now requirements. Which parts of your matcher change?
String Matching.listenFor: Separates canonicalization (casefold, NFC normalize) as a preprocessing layer from the core matcher, defines word boundaries deliberately, and warns that byte-level matching breaks on multi-byte encodings.

Topological Sort.probe: Your algorithm assumed a DAG. What does your code literally output if I feed it a cycle, and how do you turn that into detection?
Topological Sort.listenFor: Kahn's version processes fewer than V nodes — compare count to V; DFS version needs a gray/in-progress state to catch back edges; either way the cycle is reported, not silently mangled.

Topological Sort.probe: You used Kahn's algorithm. Show me the DFS version, and tell me when you'd prefer each.
Topological Sort.listenFor: Describes DFS post-order reversed as the ordering; prefers Kahn for cycle reporting, level/parallelism info, and no recursion depth issues; DFS when already doing traversal work or wanting simplicity.

Topological Sort.probe: Many valid orderings exist. The product wants the lexicographically smallest, or a deterministic one. What changes?
Topological Sort.listenFor: Swaps Kahn's plain queue for a min-heap making it O((V+E) log V); explains determinism versus smallest-order requirements and that DFS-based ordering doesn't give lexicographic control naturally.

Topological Sort.probe: This models a build system. Tasks have durations and unlimited workers — what's the minimum total completion time, and where does it come from?
Topological Sort.listenFor: Computes the critical path: longest weighted path through the DAG via DP over topological order; identifies that as the parallelism-limited lower bound, distinct from the sequential sum.

Topological Sort.probe: Edges keep being added at runtime and you must maintain a valid order incrementally. Is a full re-sort needed each time?
Topological Sort.listenFor: Knows incremental topological ordering algorithms exist (e.g. Pearce-Kelly) that locally reorder an affected region; also flags that an added edge can create a cycle and that must be detected and rejected.

Topological Sort.probe: The dependency graph doesn't fit in memory — millions of nodes across a distributed system. Sketch a realistic approach.
Topological Sort.listenFor: Partitions the graph, computes in-degrees via streaming or map-reduce style passes, processes frontier waves iteratively; acknowledges coordination costs and cites level-synchronized processing as the pattern.

Tree BFS.probe: How does your code know where one level ends and the next begins? Show me two mechanisms.
Tree BFS.listenFor: Explains capturing len(queue) before each round versus enqueueing (node, depth) pairs or sentinel markers; compares memory and cleanliness, and picks one with a stated reason.

Tree BFS.probe: What's the maximum size your queue reaches, and on what tree shape? So what's the real space complexity?
Tree BFS.listenFor: Identifies the widest level — up to n/2 nodes in a complete tree — so O(w) which is O(n) worst case; contrasts with DFS's O(h) and notes which wins depends on tree shape.

Tree BFS.probe: Zigzag order, right-side view, level averages — these are all your BFS with what small change? Generalize.
Tree BFS.listenFor: Sees the common skeleton: per-level batch processing with a pluggable per-level reduction (reverse alternately, take last element, average); proposes a levelOrder(tree, levelFn) abstraction.

Tree BFS.probe: The tree is mostly one long chain — a million nodes deep. Does BFS have any advantage here, or is it the wrong tool?
Tree BFS.listenFor: Notes the queue stays tiny but no early-exit benefit exists on a chain; recognizes BFS shines for shallowest-target searches and wide-tree level semantics, DFS/iteration may be simpler here.

Tree BFS.probe: Nodes now have parent pointers, or the 'tree' might actually contain a cycle due to a bug. How defensive is your BFS?
Tree BFS.listenFor: Adds a visited set or parent-skip when edges go both ways, bounding traversal on corrupted inputs; discusses assert-and-fail versus tolerate-and-log for structure violations in production.

Tree BFS.probe: Serialize the tree level by level, transmit it, and rebuild it. Design the format and the decoder.
Tree BFS.listenFor: Designs level-order serialization with explicit null markers, explains why nulls are required for unambiguous reconstruction, and writes the queue-driven decoder pairing parents with the next two slots.

Tree DFS.probe: Pre-, in-, or post-order — which did your solution need, and why was that the only one that works?
Tree DFS.listenFor: Ties the order to information flow: post-order when a node needs children's results, pre-order when children need ancestor context, in-order for BST sorted properties; not just definitions.

Tree DFS.probe: Your recursion returns one value but the answer might live at any node — the classic 'path through' versus 'path ending here' split. Explain how you kept those separate.
Tree DFS.listenFor: Articulates the two-quantity pattern: return the extendable-to-parent value while updating a global or carried best with the through-node combination; explains why conflating them is wrong.

Tree DFS.probe: The tree is a million nodes deep in the worst case. Your recursion dies. Give me the iterative post-order.
Tree DFS.listenFor: Produces explicit-stack post-order via two stacks, last-visited tracking, or state-tagged frames; acknowledges it's the trickiest order to convert and explains why the stack must revisit nodes.

Tree DFS.probe: How much stack memory does your DFS use on a balanced tree versus a degenerate one? What does that say about when DFS beats BFS?
Tree DFS.listenFor: States O(h): log n balanced, n degenerate; concludes DFS wins on wide shallow trees and BFS on narrow deep ones for memory, and target location drives time in search problems.

Tree DFS.probe: Now the same tree gets thousands of queries — subtree sums, node depths, ancestor checks. One DFS per query is too slow. What do you precompute?
Tree DFS.listenFor: Proposes one preprocessing DFS storing Euler tour in/out times for O(1) ancestor and subtree-range checks, prefix aggregates for subtree sums, and binary lifting for LCA; amortizes across queries.

Tree DFS.probe: Make your traversal reusable: I want callers to run arbitrary logic per node without writing recursion themselves. Design it.
Tree DFS.listenFor: Offers visitor callbacks with pre/post hooks or a generator/iterator yielding nodes lazily; discusses early termination, and how lazy iteration composes with filters without materializing the whole tree.

Trie.probe: What's the memory cost of your trie, honestly — per node and in total? Where does it hurt most?
Trie.listenFor: Accounts for per-node child containers: 26-slot arrays waste space at sparse depth, hash maps add overhead per entry; total is O(total characters) nodes worst case and mentions pointer overhead dominating payload.

Trie.probe: The alphabet is now full Unicode, not lowercase a-z. What breaks in your child storage and what do you switch to?
Trie.listenFor: Fixed 26-arrays fail; switches to hash-map children or byte-level tries over UTF-8; discusses the depth-versus-fanout consequences of byte-level decomposition.

Trie.probe: How do you delete a word from your trie — and what must you be careful not to destroy?
Trie.listenFor: Clears the terminal flag, then prunes upward only nodes with no children and no terminal mark, stopping at shared prefixes; recursive unwind or parent-stack implementation described correctly.

Trie.probe: Memory is the bottleneck. What trie compressions exist, and what do they cost you?
Trie.listenFor: Names radix/Patricia tries collapsing single-child chains, ternary search trees, or DAWG merging shared suffixes; notes added implementation complexity and harder mutation in exchange for large space savings.

Trie.probe: Compare your trie against a sorted array with binary search for the same prefix queries. When does the trie actually win?
Trie.listenFor: Sorted array gives O(m log n) prefix location with great cache behavior; trie gives O(m) and cheap incremental insertion and per-node augmentation; wins under heavy mutation or per-prefix aggregates, loses on memory.

Trie.probe: Design autocomplete on top of this: top 5 completions by popularity, updated as users type each character. What do you store where?
Trie.listenFor: Augments nodes with cached top-k lists or hot scores maintained on insert/update, walks one node per keystroke keeping a cursor, and discusses staleness versus recompute cost and fallback when the prefix leaves the trie.

Two Pointers.probe: Your pointers each move at most n steps, fine — but prove the algorithm doesn't SKIP the answer when a pointer advances.
Two Pointers.listenFor: Gives the elimination argument: when a pointer moves, every pair it abandons is provably non-optimal or invalid — e.g. in sorted two-sum, moving left past a too-small value discards only smaller sums.

Two Pointers.probe: The two-pointer trick needed sorted input. The input isn't sorted and I also need original indices in the answer. Now what?
Two Pointers.listenFor: Either sorts index-value pairs and translates back, or abandons two pointers for a hash map single pass; compares the O(n log n) versus O(n)-with-O(n)-space trade and picks deliberately.

Two Pointers.probe: Extend your pair solution to triplets, then quadruplets. What's the complexity pattern and where's the wall?
Two Pointers.listenFor: Fixes outer elements and runs two pointers inside: O(n^2) for 3-sum, O(n^3) for 4-sum; mentions duplicate-skipping at every level and that k-sum generalizes recursively with O(n^(k-1)).

Two Pointers.probe: How does your code avoid emitting duplicate pairs or triplets when the input has repeated values?
Two Pointers.listenFor: Skips over equal neighbors after processing each fixed element and after each found pair on both pointers; explains why skipping must happen at each level, not by deduplicating output afterward.

Two Pointers.probe: One array is tiny, the other is enormous and on disk — you're intersecting them. Do symmetric two pointers still make sense?
Two Pointers.listenFor: Reconsiders: binary-searching the big array per small element is O(s log L), or hashing the small array and streaming the large one; symmetric merging wastefully scans the giant array.

Two Pointers.probe: Your solution moves pointers inward from both ends. What class of problems moves them in the SAME direction instead, and how do you tell which shape you need?
Two Pointers.listenFor: Distinguishes converging pointers (pair search on sorted data, container problems) from same-direction fast/slow or read/write pointers (dedup, partitioning, windows); keys the choice to whether the answer is a pair or a contiguous region.

Union-Find.probe: You said union and find are 'basically O(1)'. What's the actual bound, and which two optimizations produce it?
Union-Find.listenFor: Names path compression plus union by rank/size yielding amortized inverse-Ackermann alpha(n); knows either alone gives O(log n) and can explain what each optimization physically does to the trees.

Union-Find.probe: Walk me through what path compression does to the structure, and why it doesn't corrupt ranks.
Union-Find.listenFor: Explains pointing every traversed node at the root flattens future finds; notes rank becomes an upper bound rather than exact height after compression, which the analysis tolerates.

Union-Find.probe: The elements aren't integers 0..n-1 — they're strings or arbitrary objects. What changes?
Union-Find.listenFor: Adds a hash map from element to index (or parent-map keyed directly by element), notes the hashing cost now dominates the alpha(n), and handles first-seen registration cleanly.

Union-Find.probe: Now I need to UN-merge — delete an edge and split components. Why is that hard, and what would you use instead?
Union-Find.listenFor: Recognizes union-find is inherently incremental — merges lose the boundary information needed to split; names offline reverse processing of deletions, or link-cut/Euler-tour trees for true dynamic connectivity.

Union-Find.probe: Besides connectivity, what per-component data can you maintain through unions — and show me how a merge updates it.
Union-Find.listenFor: Augments the root with size, min/max, sum, or count; merge combines the two roots' aggregates in O(1); mentions weighted union-find for relative-offset problems like equations division.

Union-Find.probe: Edges stream in and after each edge I need the number of components and the largest component size. What's the per-edge cost of your design?
Union-Find.listenFor: Maintains a component counter decremented on successful unions and a running max of root sizes, both O(1) on top of union; total O(E alpha(n)) and answers are available after every single edge.
